entities: the principal (the money put in at the start)
causalLinks: a higher rate adds a bigger share of the balance each period, so the balance grows faster
more periods means more rounds of interest, and each round works on a bigger balance than the last
a bigger balance makes the next interest payment bigger, which makes the balance bigger again
a bigger principal scales every later balance by the same factor
rubric.coreRule: value after n periods = principal x (1 + rate per period)^n: each period's interest is computed on the current balance, past interest included
rubric.whyRuleMatters: Interest is paid on the whole current balance, not just the original deposit, so each period's interest includes interest on earlier interest. That feedback is why the number of periods is an exponent and why growth speeds up instead of staying flat.
rubric.whyRuleQuestion: Why is the number of years an exponent in the formula, instead of a multiplier the way it is for simple interest?
rubric.anchorDescription: At the end of each year the bank adds 7% of whatever is in the account at that moment, including interest it added in earlier years.
rubric.anchorPrompt: You put in $1,000 at 7% a year. What is in the account after year 1, and after year 2? Say why year 2 adds more than year 1.

contrastingCases.label: Interest on interest
contrastingCases.detail: Alex puts $1,000 in an account that pays 7% a year on the current balance. Year 1 adds $70 (balance $1,070). Year 2 adds 7% of $1,070, which is $74.90 (balance $1,144.90). After 30 years: about $7,612.
contrastingCases.oneLine: $1,000 at 7% on the current balance: $7,612 after 30 years

contrastingCases.label: Same $70 every year
contrastingCases.detail: Sam puts $1,000 in an account that pays $70 every year, always 7% of the original $1,000. Year 1 adds $70, year 2 adds $70. After 30 years: $1,000 + 30 x $70 = $3,100.
contrastingCases.oneLine: $1,000 plus a flat $70 a year: $3,100 after 30 years

contrastingCases.label: Monthly instead of yearly
contrastingCases.detail: Jo's account pays 7% a year but splits it into twelve monthly payments of about 0.58% each, every one on the current balance. After 30 years: about $8,116, more than yearly compounding's $7,612, because interest starts earning interest sooner.
contrastingCases.oneLine: 7% split into monthly payments: $8,116 after 30 years

extremeCaseDimensions.description: push the number of periods very high (hundreds of years) and ask what the balance does
set the rate to exactly 0% for any number of periods
start with almost nothing (one cent) at a high rate for a long time
set the rate to 100% or more per period and watch a single period

confusableNeighbors.label: Simple interest
confusableNeighbors.question: How does compound interest differ from simple interest, and when do the two give the same number?
confusableNeighbors.correctDistinction: Simple interest pays a fixed share of the original principal each period, so the balance grows in a straight line; compound interest pays on the current balance, so each payment is bigger than the last. They give the same number after exactly one period, and compound pulls ahead every period after that: simple interest is the first-year slice of compound interest, repeated.

confusableNeighbors.label: APR vs APY
confusableNeighbors.question: A card says 24% APR, but the money owed grows by more than 24% in a year. Why, and which number tells you the real yearly growth?
confusableNeighbors.correctDistinction: APR is the stated rate before compounding (24% a year charged as twelve 2% monthly steps); APY is the actual yearly growth after compounding those steps, about 26.8%. APY comes from applying the compound rule to the APR's per-period rate, so the gap between them is exactly the interest on interest.

transferStructuralRequirements: a stock that carries over from one period to the next
a per-period change that is a fixed fraction of the current stock, not of the starting stock
repeated periods, so the change in one period raises the base for the next
growth that is multiplicative over time (an exponent), not additive
rubric.referenceTransferExample: A rumor in a school: each day, every person who knows it tells 10% as many new people as already know. 100 people on day 1 become 110, then 121, then 133; after 30 days about 1,745 know it, not the 400 you would get from adding 10 a day.

misconceptions.label: Interest is the same amount every year
misconceptions.tell: They work out $1,000 at 7% for 30 years as 1,000 + 30 x 70 = $3,100.
misconceptions.fix: Each year's interest is 7% of the current balance, which already holds past interest, so the yearly addition grows: the 30-year total is about $7,612.

misconceptions.label: Interest happens once
misconceptions.tell: They add 7% a single time and stop at $1,070.
misconceptions.fix: The 7% is applied every period on whatever is there, so over 30 years it is applied 30 times, each time on a bigger balance.

misconceptions.label: Rate matters, time does not
misconceptions.tell: They expect doubling the rate to matter more than doubling the years.
misconceptions.fix: Time is the exponent: at 7%, 15 years turns $1,000 into $2,759 and 30 years into $7,612. Extra years multiply the result; extra rate points only add to the base.

extremeCases.scenario: $1 at 5% a year, left alone for 500 years.
extremeCases.correctBehavior: It grows to about $39 billion; with enough periods even a small rate overwhelms any flat yearly addition.

predict.question: After all those years, what happens to the balance?

choices.text: It grows to $26, adding the same 5 cents every year.
It stops at $1.05 after one year of interest.

predict.piece: more periods let interest keep growing on a bigger balance

extremeCases.scenario: $1,000 at 0% a year, left for 40 years.
extremeCases.correctBehavior: The balance stays exactly $1,000; with nothing added there is nothing to compound.

predict.question: What happens to the balance over the 40 years?

choices.text: It gets larger because many years always make money compound.
It falls because money always changes over time.

predict.piece: with a zero rate, nothing is added to the balance

extremeCases.scenario: One cent at 10% a year for 200 years.
extremeCases.correctBehavior: It becomes about $1.9 million; the principal only scales the result, the growth factor comes from rate and time.

predict.question: What happens to this tiny starting amount after 200 years?

choices.text: It reaches 21 cents, adding the same amount each year.
It becomes 1.1 cents because interest happens once.

predict.piece: a tiny principal can still grow huge when interest has time

prediction.prompt: You put $1,000 in an account paying 7% a year on the current balance. After 30 years, how much is in the account?

extremes.watch: At 5% a year, $1,000 grows to $4,322 by year 30 and doubles about every 14 years, so even $1 swells over 500 years.
At 0% nothing is added: $1,000 is still $1,000 at year 30. A flat line, with no interest to earn interest.
At 10% a year, $1,000 becomes $17,449 by year 30; the curve bends up harder each year, so one cent grows huge over 200 years.
